nz-first.promise: Repeal the 'anti-smacking' law (Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007), or put it to a binding referendum
nz-first.made: 2011 election (party convention vow); repeated 2017 as a stated coalition condition
nz-first.detail: In 2017 NZ First said it would not support any government that opposed the policy. It then dropped the demand in its coalition negotiations with Labour. The law was not changed.

nz-first.promise: Work with parties that would buy back the state assets partly privatised by National (power companies)
nz-first.detail: NZ First stayed in opposition after 2014. When it entered government in 2017, no buy-back of the partly sold power companies was carried out.

nz-first.promise: Binding referendum on abolishing the Māori electorates (described in 2017 as a bottom line)
nz-first.detail: Peters signalled during the 2017 talks with Labour that he would drop it, and it was not in the coalition agreement. NZ First is campaigning on it again in 2026.

nz-first.promise: Binding referendum on cutting Parliament to 100 MPs
nz-first.detail: Not in the 2017 Labour–NZ First coalition agreement and not held.

nz-first.promise: Cut net immigration to about 10,000 a year (from 72,300 in the year to June 2017)
nz-first.detail: The coalition agreement contained no numerical immigration cap, and none was introduced in 2017–20. Migration fell sharply only when COVID-19 closed the border in 2020.

nz-first.promise: Bring banks back into New Zealand ownership, starting by making Kiwibank the government's banker
nz-first.detail: No bank was brought into New Zealand ownership in 2017–20. The 2017 agreement included only an investigation into capitalising Kiwibank. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning to buy back BNZ (see the 2026 entry).

nz-first.promise: Ring-fence GST to the regions where it is collected, and write off student loans for graduates who work outside the main centres
nz-first.detail: Neither policy was in the coalition agreement. The regional-development aim was pursued through the Provincial Growth Fund instead.

nz-first.promise: Raise the minimum wage to $20 an hour (final step April 2021)
nz-first.detail: The minimum wage rose to $16.50 in 2018, $18.90 in 2020 and $20.00 from April 2021, as scheduled.

nz-first.promise: 1,800 extra police over three years
nz-first.made: 2017 election / coalition agreement ('strive towards adding 1800 new police officers over three years')
nz-first.detail: On 21 November 2019 the government said 1,825 new police had been deployed since October 2017. That count was of graduates and did not net out attrition. In June 2019 Police Minister Stuart Nash had called the target 'aspirational', and the Police Association said the net gain was far smaller.

nz-first.promise: A $1 billion-a-year regional development fund (Provincial Growth Fund, $3 billion over the term)
nz-first.detail: Shane Jones administered the $3b Provincial Growth Fund. Early grants included $6m for the Whanganui rail line, $5m for the Napier–Wairoa line and $2.3m for Gisborne port. The Auditor-General (2020) questioned how jobs were counted and called for more transparency. A 2023 Auditor-General review of the fund's 'reset' could not be sure its investments represented value for money. A July 2020 claim of 13,000 jobs included many 'previous' (temporary) jobs.

nz-first.promise: Plant one billion trees by 2028
nz-first.detail: 149.4 million trees had been planted by May 2020, against an informal pace of 100 million a year. MPI's tracker counts about 801 million planted from 2018 to 30 November 2025, but only about 39 million of them were directly funded by the One Billion Trees Fund; the rest is other planting that MPI counts towards the goal. The fund is closed to new applications, and the 2028 goal looks unlikely without a sharp acceleration.

nz-first.promise: Re-establish the New Zealand Forest Service
nz-first.detail: Re-established as Te Uru Rākau (Forestry New Zealand) during the 2017–20 term.

nz-first.promise: Free doctors' visits for all under-14s
nz-first.detail: Introduced during the 2017–20 term.

nz-first.promise: Re-enter the Pike River Mine
nz-first.detail: The Pike River Recovery Agency was set up and the mine drift was re-entered.

nz-first.promise: 'Waka-jumping' law: an MP who leaves their party loses their seat
nz-first.detail: The Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act passed on 27 September 2018 and took effect on 4 October 2018. It was driven by Peters and passed with grudging Green support.

nz-first.promise: A royalty on exports of bottled water
nz-first.detail: Officials warned in 2017 that an export-only tax could breach free-trade agreements, including the CPTPP. By 2019 the government was still 'struggling to deliver', and bottled-water exports had risen sharply. No royalty was introduced. Labour's wider water levy also did not survive the coalition talks.

nz-first.promise: Feasibility study on moving the Ports of Auckland, giving Northport serious consideration, with rail and road upgrades to Northland
nz-first.made: 2017 coalition agreement (NZ First policy since at least 2017)
nz-first.detail: The Upper North Island Supply Chain Strategy working group recommended moving Ports of Auckland's freight operations to Northport, at an estimated $10.3b, and Shane Jones called it 'the King Kong of infrastructure'. In December 2019 Cabinet ordered further work instead of approving it, and the decision was deferred in 2020. The port did not move. PGF money did go to regional rail lines (Whanganui and Napier–Wairoa).

nz-first.promise: Put the End of Life Choice Act to a binding referendum (a condition of NZ First's support)
nz-first.detail: Jenny Marcroft's amendment passed 63–57 in October 2019. The referendum was held with the 2020 election and approved the Act.

nz-first.promise: A binding referendum on abortion law reform
nz-first.made: 2019 (Peters' demand during the Abortion Legislation Bill)
nz-first.detail: Justice Minister Andrew Little refused the demand. The Abortion Legislation Act passed in March 2020 without a referendum; 7 of NZ First's 9 MPs voted against it.

nz-first.promise: No comprehensive capital gains tax
nz-first.detail: On 17 April 2019 Ardern ruled out a CGT, citing the lack of agreement from NZ First and the lack of a mandate. Peters said there was 'neither a compelling rationale nor mandate'. Tax Working Group chair Sir Michael Cullen had expected an NZ First veto.

nz-first.promise: Review Parliament's processes to reflect MMP
nz-first.detail: A July 2020 report card on the NZ First agreement marked this 'No'.

nz-first.promise: Keep the NZ Super age at 65
nz-first.detail: National dropped its plan to raise the age gradually, and the age remains 65.

nz-first.promise: No foreign buyer tax (and no return of foreign buyers to the housing market)
nz-first.detail: National's proposed foreign buyer tax, which was meant to help fund its tax cuts, was dropped in the NZ First agreement. The tax cuts were funded through reprioritisation and other revenue instead.

nz-first.promise: A $1.2 billion Regional Infrastructure Fund
nz-first.detail: Established and run by Shane Jones, with $900m capital (loans and equity) and $300m operating (grants). As at 31 July 2026: $1,070.53m committed, $857.95m approved, $153.38m actually paid out, and 12 projects completed. It included more than $20m to recommission diesel storage at the former Marsden Point refinery site (April 2026).

nz-first.promise: Disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority)
nz-first.made: 2023 election / coalition agreements (shared with National and ACT)
nz-first.detail: The disestablishment law passed on 28 February 2024.

nz-first.promise: Repeal Labour's smokefree generation and denicotinisation law
nz-first.detail: Repealed on 28 February 2024.

nz-first.promise: Train 500 new police officers within two years
nz-first.detail: The deadline was missed. In April 2025 Peters said it might be 'a few weeks late'. By November 2025 the target date had been moved for the fourth time, to September 2026, and Treasury said even that would require 'significant catch up'. Luxon called it a 'stretch goal'. Labour, citing Police Association figures, said officer numbers had fallen at one point.

nz-first.promise: Make English an official language of New Zealand
nz-first.detail: The English Language Act 2026 passed on 30 July 2026, supported by the coalition parties and Labour.

nz-first.promise: Government departments to use English primary names and communicate primarily in English (except Māori-specific agencies)
nz-first.detail: Ministers ordered English-first names from December 2023 (for example, Waka Kotahi became NZ Transport Agency first). English was given precedence on the passport cover in July 2025, and the school lunch programme's Māori name was dropped in October 2025. Critics described the changes as anti-Māori.

nz-first.promise: Restore the right to local referendums on Māori wards
nz-first.detail: The law passed on 30 July 2024. Polls were held with the October 2025 local elections in 42 councils, and most voted to remove their wards: 24 according to Wikipedia and Te Ao Māori News, 25 in some other tallies. Nationally, more votes were cast to keep the wards than to remove them.

nz-first.promise: Review all legislation (except settlements) referring to the 'principles of the Treaty', replacing or repealing the references
nz-first.detail: In April 2026 Cabinet began weakening or removing Treaty-principles clauses in about 19–23 laws, against Ministry of Justice advice. Shane Jones sat on the ministerial oversight group. In May and July 2026 the Waitangi Tribunal found that the education-law changes breached Treaty principles and urged a pause.

nz-first.promise: A broader independent inquiry into the COVID-19 response
nz-first.detail: The existing Royal Commission's scope was widened in 2024 into a second phase, covering vaccines, mandates and lockdowns. NZ First invoked 'agree to disagree' in mid-2024 over keeping the first phase and its chair. The phase-two report, released on 10 March 2026, broadly endorsed vaccine use. NZ First then called for a further inquiry into vaccine injuries.

nz-first.promise: Remove 'gender ideology' from schools; withdraw the relationships and sexuality education guidelines
nz-first.detail: The Ministry of Education removed the guidelines in February 2025, and consultation on a replacement curriculum began in April 2025. Sport NZ was told to scrap its transgender-inclusion guidelines in July 2025. NZ First welcomed the November 2025 suspension of new puberty-blocker prescriptions; the High Court ruled those regulations unlawful on 21 October 2026.

nz-first.promise: Move Fees Free from the first year of tertiary study to the final year
nz-first.detail: Implemented from 1 January 2025. In May 2026 Peters and Finance Minister Nicola Willis confirmed that final-year Fees Free would be scrapped in Budget 2026.

nz-first.promise: A one-stop-shop fast-track consenting regime for infrastructure and development
nz-first.detail: The Fast-track Approvals Act was passed in December 2024 with 149 listed projects, and applications opened on 7 February 2025. Shane Jones is one of the three referring ministers. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning to amend it: restoring ministers' final say and requiring infrastructure planning in residential projects.

nz-first.promise: Reverse the 2018 ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration
nz-first.detail: The Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025, introduced by Resources Minister Shane Jones, passed on 31 July 2025. NZ First had been part of the Labour-led government that imposed the ban in 2018.

nz-first.promise: Investigate reopening the Marsden Point refinery, a dry dock and a rail link to Northport
nz-first.detail: The refinery has not reopened. The Regional Infrastructure Fund committed more than $20m (April 2026) to recommission diesel storage tanks holding 90 million litres at the Marsden Point terminal. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning for a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point.

nz-first.promise: Move the Ports of Auckland and the Devonport naval base to Northport; extend the main trunk line to Marsden Point
nz-first.detail: The port and naval-base move was not in the coalition agreement, which instead committed to investigating the refinery, a dry dock and the rail link.

nz-first.promise: Designate all gangs as terrorist organisations
nz-first.detail: Not adopted. The government instead banned gang patches and made gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing (September 2024).

nz-first.promise: Make gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing
nz-first.detail: Passed on 19 September 2024 alongside the gang patch ban, with coalition support.

nz-first.promise: Withdraw New Zealand from the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
nz-first.detail: Not adopted. The coalition agreement instead committed to halting work on the He Puapua report and confirming that UNDRIP has no binding legal effect in New Zealand.

nz-first.promise: Single-sex toilets law (Fair Access to Bathrooms Bill)
nz-first.made: 2023 election (16 August 2023); member's bill introduced 10 May 2024
nz-first.detail: RNZ reported on 22 April 2025 that NZ First had withdrawn the bill. It was replaced by Jenny Marcroft's bill defining 'woman' and 'man' in law, which passed its first reading on 20 May 2026 with National and ACT support.

nz-first.promise: A specific 'coward punch' offence and tougher penalties for assaulting first responders and corrections officers
nz-first.detail: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed both measures in June 2025. Their final legislative status has not been verified here.

nz-first.promise: Binding referendum on the future of the Māori electorates
nz-first.detail: This revives the 2017 promise that NZ First dropped in coalition talks. Te Pāti Māori called it 'race baiting', and Labour called it 'cheap and cynical'.

nz-first.promise: Only New Zealand citizens to vote; NZ Super only for citizens from 2029
nz-first.detail: Currently permanent residents can vote after one year's residence. A Curia poll in August 2026 found 59% support for limiting voting to citizens.

nz-first.promise: Repeal the Regulatory Standards Act 2025
nz-first.detail: Announced a week after NZ First voted the Act through its third reading. Peters said NZ First had supported it only because it was in ACT's coalition agreement.

nz-first.promise: Split the big power companies' generation and retail arms; split Foodstuffs into two national co-operatives
nz-first.detail: Both are headline cost-of-living policies.

nz-first.promise: Buy back BNZ and merge it with Kiwibank as a Crown-owned 'National Bank of New Zealand'; enrol newborn citizens in KiwiSaver
nz-first.detail: This revives NZ First's 2017 'Kiwi ownership of banks' goal. Meanwhile the National-led government allowed Kiwibank's parent to raise up to $500m from New Zealand investors (approved July 2025).

nz-first.promise: 'Kiwi Kids Grant': $5,000 a year for a child's first three years (up to three children)
nz-first.detail: A natalist family policy.

nz-first.promise: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal (replacing it with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission)
nz-first.detail: NZ First's version is faster and more absolute than ACT's (ACT would abolish the Tribunal once historical claims are settled).

mana.promise: Government-funded breakfast and lunch programmes in all decile 1 and 2 schools ('Feed the Kids' bill)
mana.detail: Hone Harawira's Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in Schools) Amendment Bill was drawn from the member's ballot on 8 November 2012 but did not become law while Mana held its seat; Mana left Parliament in 2014. (Mana was in opposition and could not pass it alone.)

mana.promise: Stop the sale of state-owned energy companies
mana.detail: Outcome not achieved: the National-led government's mixed-ownership sell-downs of Genesis, Meridian and Mighty River Power went ahead. Mana was in opposition.

mana.promise: Internet Party–Mana memorandum: Mana to hold list places 1, 3 and 4 and the parties to review the arrangement within five weeks of the election
mana.detail: List ordered as agreed; after reviews the alliance was dissolved on 13 December 2014.

mana.promise: Memorandum with the Māori Party: Mana not to contest other Māori electorates in exchange for a clear run in Te Tai Tokerau
mana.detail: Mana stood only in Te Tai Tokerau and Māngere; Harawira lost Te Tai Tokerau to Kelvin Davis 12,673 to 7,866.

united-future.promise: Peter Dunne to be Minister of Revenue and Associate Minister of Health outside Cabinet
united-future.made: 2008 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Appointed in 2008 and held the roles until resigning on 7 June 2013.

united-future.promise: Government to support United Future's income-splitting legislation to first reading
united-future.made: 2008 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: The Taxation (Income-sharing Tax Credit) Bill passed its first reading 64-54 in September 2010.

united-future.promise: No sale of any part of Kiwibank or Radio New Zealand
united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Neither was sold; Kiwibank remains wholly state-owned and RNZ a Crown entity.

united-future.promise: Statutory limit: no more than 49% of shares in public assets sold to private interests, with limits on single-entity ownership
united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Under the mixed-ownership model the Crown kept 51% of Genesis, Meridian, Mighty River Power and Air New Zealand; the Solid Energy sell-down was dropped.

united-future.promise: Pass the Game Animal Council legislation to establish the Council as a statutory body
united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National (first sought in 2008)
united-future.detail: The Game Animal Council Bill went through Parliament in 2012-13 and the Council was established as a statutory body. (Act title 'Game Animal Council Act 2013' from general knowledge; legislation.govt.nz not fetchable from the research environment.)

united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: The bill was reinstated but never had a second reading; income splitting was never enacted.

united-future.promise: Government discussion document investigating United Future's 'Flexi-Superannuation' proposal
united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Finance Minister Bill English released the discussion document in August 2013 (NZ Super from any age 60-70 at adjusted rates). Treasury later advised against proceeding and the policy itself was never adopted.

united-future.promise: Restructure the Families Commission (single commissioner, monitoring/evaluation/research functions, Families Status Report)
united-future.made: 2011 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Families Commission Amendment Act 2014 (third reading 24 March 2014, 64-56) created Superu. Labour disestablished Superu in 2018.

united-future.promise: Support public-private partnerships for major roads, in particular Transmission Gully
united-future.detail: Transmission Gully was procured as a PPP (Wellington Gateway Partnership); construction began 8 September 2014 and it opened in 2022, later and costlier than planned.

united-future.promise: Peter Dunne to be Minister of Internal Affairs, Associate Minister of Health and Associate Minister of Conservation outside Cabinet
united-future.made: 2014 confidence and supply agreement with National
united-future.detail: Served 2014-2017; extended passport validity to 10 years and led creation of Fire and Emergency New Zealand.

green.promise: A Zero Carbon Act setting a net-zero 2050 target, plus an independent Climate Change Commission
green.made: 2017 election; Labour–Green confidence and supply agreement (Oct 2017)
green.detail: This was the Greens' central 2017 demand, and it was written into the support agreement. James Shaw, as Minister for Climate Change, introduced the bill on 8 May 2019. It passed on 7 November 2019 with almost unanimous support. Shaw had to accept a compromise: biogenic methane got a separate, weaker target of 24–47% below 2017 levels by 2050, instead of net zero. The framework still stands. However, on 13 October 2025 the National-led government lowered the methane target to 14–24%.

green.promise: A referendum on legalising personal cannabis use by the 2020 election
green.made: 2017 election; Labour–Green confidence and supply agreement
green.detail: The referendum was held with the general election on 17 October 2020, so the commitment was met. The proposal was defeated: in the official count about 50.7% voted against and about 48.8% in favour. Recreational cannabis therefore stayed illegal. The Greens' 2026 platform still calls for decriminalising personal use.

green.promise: Legal access to medicinal cannabis
green.made: 2017 election (Green member's bill inherited by Chlöe Swarbrick from Julie Anne Genter)
green.detail: The Green member's bill was defeated at its first reading in January 2018. The government's own medicinal cannabis law passed in December 2018. Swarbrick then worked on the regulations that followed. The outcome was delivered, but in a narrower form than the Greens proposed.

green.promise: Make drug checking (pill testing) legal
green.detail: In late 2021 New Zealand became the first country to make drug checking permanently legal, after temporary legislation in 2020. The law was a Labour government measure, passed while the Greens were in the cooperation agreement. We could not retrieve a source in this pass that credits the change specifically to Swarbrick or to the Greens, so treat the attribution as unconfirmed.

green.promise: Light rail to Auckland Airport
green.made: 2017 election (Labour pledge; light rail and rail/cycling investment were in the Labour–Green agreement)
green.detail: No line was built in six years of Labour-led government (2017–23). In January 2022 the government endorsed a $14.6 billion tunnelled scheme, and Auckland Light Rail Ltd was set up. The incoming National-led government stopped the project in November 2023. A Cabinet paper said about $228m had been spent 'without a metre of track laid'. The main responsibility lay with Labour ministers, but the Greens had campaigned on the project and it was in their agreement.

green.promise: A 'Green Transport Card' to cut public transport costs for people on low incomes
green.detail: It came late and in a smaller form. Half-price public transport for everyone was a temporary cost-of-living measure in 2022–23. In February 2023 the government made discounted fares permanent for Community Services Card holders and tertiary students, from 1 July 2023. That was close to six years after the agreement.

green.promise: Overhaul the welfare system: remove 'excessive' sanctions and substantially lift incomes
green.made: 2017 election (Metiria Turei's welfare policy); Labour–Green agreement
green.detail: Main benefits rose by $25 a week from April 2020. From 2021 they were indexed to wages, and Budget 2021 added a further $32–55 a week, fully in place by 2022. RNZ reported this reversed the 1991 benefit cuts in real terms. The agreement also promised to remove 'excessive' sanctions; we did not verify in this pass how many were removed. The rises still fell well short of what the Greens campaigned for: a large benefit rise in 2017, and a $385-a-week Guaranteed Minimum Income in 2023. Green critics inside and outside the party said the Greens accepted too little.

green.promise: Warm, dry rental homes (healthy homes standards)
green.detail: The Healthy Homes Guarantee Act 2017 was a Labour bill that the Greens supported. It passed in the government's first months and requires rental homes to meet heating, insulation and ventilation standards.

green.promise: Stronger renters' rights, including limits on rent rises and an end to no-cause evictions
green.detail: Labour's 2020 tenancy law banned rental bidding and ended no-cause evictions. It limited rent increases to once every 12 months, but did not cap their size, which the Greens wanted. The National-led government restored 90-day no-cause terminations in December 2024. For 2026 the Greens are again promising a cap on annual rent rises (2%) and a rental warrant of fitness.

green.promise: Re-establish a Mental Health Commission
green.detail: Following the mental health inquiry, the government created Te Hiringa Mahara, the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission.

green.promise: Double the refugee quota
green.made: 2017 election ('Greens would double refugee quota as priority')
green.detail: In September 2018 the government announced the quota would rise to 1,500 a year from 2020. Labour had joined the 'Double the Quota' campaign. Resettlement was then paused at the COVID-19 border closure and restarted in 2021. The Greens' 2026 platform promises a further increase.

green.promise: End new offshore oil and gas exploration
green.detail: In April 2018 the government banned new offshore oil and gas exploration permits. Shaw called it the 'nuclear-free moment of our generation'. The decision was Labour's, in a government the Greens supported.

green.promise: Bring agriculture into emissions pricing (pricing of farm emissions by 2025)
green.made: 2017 Green climate policy (Kiwi Climate Fund); government pledge in 2019 while Shaw was Climate Change Minister
green.detail: The 2019 government pledge was to price farm emissions by 2025. No price was in place when Labour left office in 2023. In June 2024 the National-led government confirmed it would keep agriculture out of the ETS. The Greens never had the numbers to force this, but it was the main gap in Shaw's climate record. The 2017 'Kiwi Climate Fund' dividend was never adopted.

green.promise: Strengthen New Zealand's 2030 Paris target (Shaw as Climate Change Minister)
green.made: 2020–23 cooperation agreement (Shaw kept the climate portfolio)
green.detail: In October 2021, before the Glasgow COP26 summit, the government raised its 2030 target from a 30% to a 50% cut in net emissions relative to 2005 gross emissions. How much of the target will be met by buying offshore emission reductions rather than cutting emissions at home remained contested.

green.promise: Incentives to switch to clean vehicles (Clean Car Discount / feebate)
green.detail: The Clean Car Discount ran from July 2021 to 31 December 2023. Low-emission vehicles got rebates, funded by fees on high emitters. EVs rose from about 6% of new car sales when it started to about 27% by the end of 2023. The National-led government repealed it under urgency on 14 December 2023, against the votes of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. The scheme was delivered, then reversed by the next government.

green.promise: Oppose 'waka-jumping' laws that let party leaders expel MPs from Parliament
green.made: Long-standing Green position (opposed the 1999, 2001 and 2005 bills)
green.detail: Bound by its 2017 agreement to let the Labour–NZ First coalition deal be implemented, the Green caucus voted for the Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Bill at every stage in 2018. It passed 63–57. A party spokesperson said the negotiators 'forgot' to register the Greens' opposition. Former co-leader Jeanette Fitzsimons publicly opposed the bill. In 2020 the Greens voted for a National bill to repeal the law (NZ First's Winston Peters called them 'untrustworthy'), and they voted for repeal again in 2021. In October 2024 the Greens used the same law to expel Darleen Tana from Parliament.

green.promise: No state funding for private schools (Green education policy)
green.detail: In August 2020 Shaw, as Associate Finance Minister, secured $11.7m from the COVID 'shovel-ready' fund for the private Green School in Taranaki. Newshub reported he had refused to sign off the $3b package unless the school was included. Former Green MPs called it a betrayal. Shaw apologised for an 'error of judgment', and in November 2020 the grant was converted into a loan.

green.promise: A wealth tax
green.detail: Not delivered. During the campaign Jacinda Ardern ruled out a wealth tax while she was Prime Minister. Labour then won an outright majority, and the 2020 cooperation agreement did not include one. The Greens had no leverage. They have campaigned for a wealth tax at every election since.

green.promise: 2023 tax plan: 2.5% wealth tax on net assets over $2m ($4m for couples), 45% top rate over $180,000, and a $385-a-week Guaranteed Minimum Income
green.detail: Not delivered: the Greens went into opposition. The 2026 tax plan, released early by mistake on 21 June 2026, is much less ambitious, and the NZ Herald said the party had 'dramatically reined in' its plans. The wealth tax now applies only to assets over $10m. The new top bracket starts at $160,000, and a $10,000 tax-free threshold remains. A broad commitment to raise benefits continues.

green.promise: Will not seek to govern with National
green.made: 2017 election aftermath (Shaw); repeated in every campaign since
green.detail: Shaw ruled out talks with National in 2017, and the Greens have only ever supported Labour-led governments. In February 2026 Hipkins, Swarbrick and Davidson announced at Waitangi that Labour and the Greens would work together in the campaign and in a future government. (The Greens did sign a policy memorandum of understanding with National in 2009, without giving it confidence and supply.)

green.promise: Restore New Zealand citizenship to Samoans born 1924–1949 (Teanau Tuiono's member's bill)
green.detail: Tuiono's Restoring Citizenship bill passed into law on 20 November 2024 with unanimous support from all parties. It is the Greens' most significant legislative win from opposition.

green.promise: A 'right to repair' law (Marama Davidson's member's bill)
green.detail: It passed its first reading on 19 February 2025 with Green, Labour, Te Pāti Māori and NZ First votes. NZ First later withdrew its support at select committee, so the bill no longer had a majority. Davidson also apologised in October 2025 for missing the bill's member's-day speaking slot. It has not passed.

green.promise: Revoke coal, gold and seabed-mining consents granted under the Fast-track Approvals Act, and repeal the Act
green.detail: A pledge for a future government. The Greens told mining companies they were 'on notice'.

green.promise: 2026 tax plan: 2.5% tax on net wealth over $10m, an inheritance tax, a 33% company rate for big corporations, a new bracket over $160,000 and a $10,000 tax-free threshold
green.detail: Pitched as tackling 'inequality and corporate greed' and paying for income-tax cuts for lower earners. National ran a social-media attack video claiming the Greens would tax income over $160,000 at 45%. Swarbrick said the video misrepresented the policy and called it 'AI slop'; National declined to remove it.

green.promise: Cap annual rent increases (2%), create a rental warrant of fitness and build tens of thousands of public homes
green.detail: The Greens have pushed for rent caps since at least 2020. Labour did not adopt them in 2017–23.

green.promise: 'KiwiMart': a government-owned supermarket chain made up of 120 stores and two distribution centres that Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell
green.detail: Pitched as a way to break the supermarket duopoly.

green.promise: 'Kiwipower', a new Crown entity investing in renewable generation to cut power bills, and 'electrify everything'
green.detail: Developed after the 2026 fuel shock linked to the Iran war.

green.promise: Restore the previous free school lunches scheme and expand it to about 400 more schools
green.detail: This would reverse the coalition's cheaper redesign of Ka Ora, Ka Ako.

green.promise: Restore pay equity and fund a settlement of at least $4.5b for 65,000 care and support workers
green.detail: Responds to the coalition's 2025 changes to the pay-equity regime.

green.promise: $4b for intercity passenger rail (an overnight Auckland–Wellington service, Christchurch–Dunedin trains, Te Huia extended to Tauranga)
green.detail: Comes alongside promises of fare-free public transport for young people, disabled people and Community Services Card holders, and a $2 adult fare cap.

green.promise: Cap political donations at $30,000, ban corporate donations, create a lobbying register and require a two-year stand-down before ministers can become lobbyists
green.detail: Builds on Golriz Ghahraman's Electoral (Strengthening Democracy) bill, which was defeated in 2022.

green.promise: Automatic (default) union membership for new workers
green.detail: Taken to the election as a member's bill.

te-pati-maori.promise: Repeal the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 and restore Māori access to the courts for customary title
te-pati-maori.made: Founding kaupapa (2004); 2008 National–Māori Party confidence and supply agreement
te-pati-maori.detail: The party was founded over this issue. In the 2008 agreement National committed only to review the 2004 Act. The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 replaced it and passed 63–56, supported by National, the Māori Party and United Future. Labour, the Greens, ACT and Hone Harawira voted against. The new Act restored the right to go to court for customary title. Tariana Turia backed it while calling it 'drafted by politics, rather than what is fair and moral'. Harawira quit the party over the compromise and formed Mana. In October 2025 the National-led government's amendment raised the legal test for customary marine title. Te Pāti Māori opposed it, and its MPs burned a copy outside Parliament.

te-pati-maori.promise: Protect (and entrench) the Māori electorates
te-pati-maori.detail: National had campaigned on abolishing the Māori seats. In the 2008 agreement it promised not to remove them 'without the consent of the Māori people', and it kept that promise. The seats still exist in 2026. Entrenchment, the Māori Party's own aim, was shelved: both parties agreed they would 'not be pursuing the entrenchment of the Māori seats this parliamentary term'.

te-pati-maori.promise: A review of constitutional arrangements, including Māori representation
te-pati-maori.detail: The review began in 2011 as a commitment under the agreement. We found no evidence in this pass that it led to significant constitutional change. Te Pāti Māori's 2026 programme (Mātike Mai, a Te Tiriti Commission, a 2040 target) shows the party sees this as unfinished business.

te-pati-maori.promise: Whānau Ora: whānau-centred, Māori-led delivery of health and social services
te-pati-maori.made: 2008 agreement (Turia's flagship); made a cornerstone of the 2011 agreement
te-pati-maori.detail: Announced in April 2010 with Turia as Minister for Whānau Ora. Three commissioning agencies were set up in 2014. It is the party's most lasting policy achievement. Critics, including Winston Peters, said its outcomes were hard to measure and that funding was concentrated in Turia's electorate. In 2025 the National-led government re-tendered the contracts, and the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, led by party president John Tamihere, lost its contract. Te Puni Kōkiri also ordered a review into whether Whānau Ora money had been used for 'electioneering', namely an advertising campaign urging Māori to join the Māori roll.

te-pati-maori.promise: New Zealand to support the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP)
te-pati-maori.made: Māori Party policy; secured during the 2008–11 term
te-pati-maori.detail: Pita Sharples, as Māori Affairs Minister, announced New Zealand's support at the UN Permanent Forum on 20 April 2010. Under Labour in 2007, New Zealand had been one of four countries to vote against the declaration. Sharples credited the National–Māori Party relationship. Support was for a 'non-binding' declaration. Making UNDRIP enforceable remains a 2026 Te Pāti Māori goal.

te-pati-maori.promise: Cut smoking (Turia's tobacco agenda): higher tobacco excise, plain packaging, Smokefree 2025
te-pati-maori.detail: In 2011 the government adopted a Smokefree 2025 goal, with steep excise increases and later plain packaging, all led by Turia. A separate Labour smokefree-generation law (2022) was repealed by the National-led government in February 2024, which Te Pāti Māori opposed.

te-pati-maori.promise: A new Māori language law giving Māori a stronger role in revitalising te reo
te-pati-maori.made: 2014 confidence and supply term (Te Ururoa Flavell as Minister for Māori Development)
te-pati-maori.detail: Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 (the Māori Language Act 2016) set up Te Mātāwai to act for iwi and Māori on language revitalisation. It was enacted in both te reo Māori and English, a first for New Zealand.

te-pati-maori.promise: Reform Māori land law (Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill)
te-pati-maori.detail: Flavell's bill was introduced in 2016. It proved controversial and did not pass before the 2017 election. The new Labour minister withdrew it. Smaller targeted amendments passed in 2020.

te-pati-maori.promise: Recognition of the New Zealand Wars
te-pati-maori.detail: A national day of commemoration for the New Zealand Wars began in 2017 and is held on 28 October. It followed a 2015 petition from Ōtorohanga College students. After the 2017 defeat, Marama Fox credited Flavell with this, with the pardon of Rua Kenana, and with UNDRIP support. The Māori Party was one of several actors involved.

te-pati-maori.promise: Win back the Māori electorates through an electoral pact with Mana (2017)
te-pati-maori.made: February 2017 (the Māori Party stood aside in Te Tai Tokerau for Hone Harawira)
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour won all seven Māori seats in 2017. Flavell lost Waiariki, and the party left Parliament on 1.18% of the party vote. Metro magazine and others put the defeat down to a backlash against nine years of supporting National.

te-pati-maori.promise: An independent Māori Health Authority
te-pati-maori.detail: Te Pāti Māori was not in government, but Labour created Te Aka Whai Ora, a Māori Health Authority, in its 2022 health reforms. The National-led government abolished it under urgency on 28 February 2024. The 2026 platform promises 'investment in Māori health outcomes'.

te-pati-maori.promise: No coalition with the right (National/ACT)
te-pati-maori.detail: This reversed the party's 2008–17 approach of working with National. Te Pāti Māori stayed in opposition after 2023. In 2026 it is asking supporters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to Labour or the Greens, to remove the coalition.

te-pati-maori.promise: Disclose political donations as the law requires
te-pati-maori.detail: In April 2021 the Electoral Commission referred the party to Police for failing to disclose about $320,000 of donations in time. They included $158,224 from then co-leader John Tamihere and $120,000 from Aotearoa Te Kahu LP. Police passed the case to the Serious Fraud Office, which closed it in 2022 without charges. The party blamed volunteers who did not know the rules. In 2022 Charities Services also examined loans and payments to Tamihere's 2020 campaigns from charities he leads (Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust, NUMA).

te-pati-maori.promise: Stand candidates in general (non-Māori) electorates at the 2026 election
te-pati-maori.detail: By October 2026 the party was standing only seven candidates, one in each Māori electorate. Its party list has one name, party secretary Lance Norman. This fits its strategic-voting call, but it reverses the 2025 announcement.

te-pati-maori.promise: Contest all seven Māori electorates in 2026
te-pati-maori.detail: Candidates are standing in all seven seats, including Aperahama Edwards in Te Tai Tokerau and Lisa Marie Murch in Te Tai Tonga. Those two electorate committees had resigned in support of Kapa-Kingi and Ferris. The party is up against two of its own former MPs: Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau Party) and Tākuta Ferris (independent).

te-pati-maori.promise: A Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with power to audit and veto non-compliant bills, as a coalition 'bottom line'
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour's Chris Hipkins said he would not support a commissioner able to overturn laws, though he was open to better 'checks and balances'. The 2026 package of 1 September 2026 proposes an independent Te Tiriti Commission to investigate Crown breaches, binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations, a 2040 constitutional-reform target and a $200m Mātike Mai fund. Labour has ruled out the Commission and Mātike Mai. We found no 2026 source confirming whether the veto power or the 'bottom line' status still stands.

te-pati-maori.promise: Abolish prisons by 2040 in favour of community-led solutions
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour said it was 'dead-set against' the policy.

te-pati-maori.promise: 'Kiwi Tax Plan': a 48% rate on income over $300,000, a rebate for people earning under $30,000, a wealth tax, a higher company tax rate, land-banking and vacant-home taxes, a 5% stamp duty and no GST on kai
te-pati-maori.made: 2026 election (26 August 2026); largely repeats the 2023 tax plan
te-pati-maori.detail: This is very close to the 2023 package (zero tax under $30,000, 48% over $300,000, 33% company tax, a wealth tax, GST off food), which shows consistency over time. None of it was enacted in 2023–26, when the party was in opposition.

te-pati-maori.promise: A $1 billion fund for Māori and community ownership of new renewable energy ('energy sovereignty')
Give Māori collectives Crown-owned land and $100m to set up supermarket chains
A $200m Takatāpui Commission
te-pati-maori.detail: RNZ reported the pledge as '$200 million to change who holds power for decisions about takatāpui' (Māori LGBTQ+ people). Check the exact powers proposed in the party's policy document.

labour.promise: Introduce a capital gains tax (excluding the family home)
labour.detail: Labour campaigned on a CGT in 2011 and again in 2014 but lost both elections. Andrew Little's leadership dropped it (confirmed at the 2015 conference); Ardern revived it via the Tax Working Group in 2017-19 then ruled it out (2019); Hipkins ruled it out in 2023, then Labour adopted a narrower property CGT for 2026.

labour.promise: Raise the NZ Superannuation eligibility age from 65 to 67 (phased 2020-2033)
labour.detail: A signature 'responsible' policy under Goff and Cunliffe. Little dropped it after taking over in 2014 and said in 2017 the age would not rise 'while I'm leader'. Labour in government (2017-23) kept the age at 65 and resumed Super Fund contributions.

labour.promise: Remove GST from fresh fruit and vegetables
labour.detail: Dropped under David Cunliffe (along with the $5,000 tax-free threshold) before 2014. The same idea was revived by Hipkins in 2023 (see 2023 entry).

labour.promise: Make KiwiSaver compulsory, with employer contributions rising to 7%
labour.detail: Not carried into the 2017 platform or enacted 2017-23. In 2026 Labour again proposes compulsory employer contributions and a higher minimum contribution (see 2026 entries).

labour.promise: Create 'NZ Power', a single buyer of wholesale electricity (joint Labour-Green policy)
labour.detail: Shelved by Andrew Little after the 2014 defeat; never revived.

labour.promise: Set up KiwiAssure, a state-owned general insurer alongside Kiwibank
labour.detail: Put under review by Little in 2015; not in the 2017 platform and never established.

labour.promise: Raise the top income tax rate to 36 cents for income over $150,000
labour.detail: Dropped after 2014; Little said in 2017 Labour had no plans to raise income taxes. Labour later introduced a 39% rate on income over $180,000 in 2021 (see 2020 entry).

labour.promise: Deliver the 100-day plan (fees-free year, Healthy Homes, foreign-buyer ban, Families Package, stop state-house sales, child poverty bill, mental health inquiry, Tax Working Group, Pike River agency, etc.)
labour.detail: RNZ's and 1News' tracking concluded the list was largely ticked off by early February 2018. Several items were 'delivered' by introducing a bill or starting an inquiry rather than finishing it (e.g. the child poverty bill, the employment-law changes). One item was swapped after coalition talks.

labour.promise: First year of tertiary study or training fees-free from 1 January 2018
labour.detail: Delivered on time. An AUT study using Stats NZ data on 250,000+ school leavers found no clear increase in tertiary participation after allowing for prior trends. The coalition government converted it to final-year fees-free from 2025.

labour.promise: Extend fees-free tertiary education to three years by 2024
labour.detail: In September 2020 Chris Hipkins (Education Minister) announced Labour would not extend fees-free beyond the first year, redirecting money to free apprenticeships/targeted vocational training. Students' associations called it a broken promise.

labour.promise: Raise student allowances and living-cost loans by $50 a week
labour.detail: Took effect 1 January 2018.

labour.promise: Pass the Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill so all rentals are warm and dry
labour.detail: Healthy Homes Guarantee Act passed December 2017; standards set 2019. Compliance deadlines were later pushed out (private landlords: from 1 July 2024 to 1 July 2025; Kāinga Ora from 2023 to 2024) by Labour itself in 2022.

labour.promise: Ban overseas speculators from buying existing homes
labour.detail: Overseas Investment Amendment Act passed 15 August 2018 (65-57), in force 22 October 2018. Australians and Singaporeans exempt because of trade agreements. The 2023-26 coalition kept the ban but in 2025 created an exemption for Active Investor Plus visa holders buying homes worth $5m+.

labour.promise: Stop the sale of state houses and build more public housing (1,000+ state houses a year)
labour.detail: State-house sales stopped. Labour reported a net increase of 10,037 public homes Oct 2017-June 2022 (8,240 new builds) and claimed 13,000+ by 2023, 'the most since the 1950s'. Critics (National; Newshub explainer) note many 'places' were purchases/leases and a ~5,000-home pipeline was inherited; AAP FactCheck found both parties can claim some credit.

labour.promise: KiwiBuild: build 100,000 affordable homes over 10 years
labour.detail: Interim targets missed badly (1,000 homes by June 2019 was cut to 300; ~258 built by mid-2019; 452 by June 2020). In the September 2019 'reset' Megan Woods scrapped the 100,000 target altogether. Kāinga Ora reported 2,335 KiwiBuild homes completed between July 2018 and 29 February 2024, plus 1,238 contracted.

labour.promise: KiwiBuild: 1,000 homes in the first year (to June 2019)
labour.detail: Target cut to 300 in January 2019, then all interim targets dropped by May 2019. 2019 had been branded the 'Year of Delivery'.

labour.promise: Light rail from Auckland CBD to Mt Roskill within four years and to the airport within ten
labour.detail: No track was laid. The process switched between NZTA, an unsolicited NZ Infra (NZ Super Fund/CDPQ) bid and a light-metro option; NZ First blocked a decision in 2020. In January 2022 Labour (now governing alone) endorsed a $14.6b tunnelled line; the National-led government cancelled it in January 2024, citing $228m spent (figure disputed by Labour's Michael Wood).

labour.promise: Reduce net migration by 20,000-30,000 a year
labour.detail: No cut was made before COVID: net migration reached a record ~91,700 gain in the year to early 2020. The later drop was caused by COVID border closures, not the 2017 policy. By 2022 ministers declined to restate the numerical goal.

labour.promise: Families Package: Best Start payment, Winter Energy Payment, higher Working for Families and Accommodation Supplement (funded by cancelling National's tax cuts)
labour.detail: Legislated December 2017, in force 1 July 2018; projected to lift 88,000 children out of poverty by 2020/21.

labour.promise: Extend paid parental leave to 26 weeks by 2020
labour.detail: 22 weeks from 1 July 2018 and 26 weeks from 1 July 2020, as scheduled.

labour.promise: Legislate child poverty reduction targets and (Ardern) halve child poverty within 10 years
labour.detail: Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 passed with near-unanimous support. Of the first three-year targets (2020/21) two of three were met (after-housing-costs low income and material hardship); the before-housing-costs target was missed. Material hardship then rose from 10.5% (2021/22) to 12.5% (2022/23) amid high inflation, and the Auditor-General reported none of the 2023/24 targets were met. 10-year targets (2027/28) remain unmet on current Treasury modelling.

labour.promise: Hold a mental health inquiry and act on it (Budget 2019 $1.9b mental wellbeing package)
labour.detail: Inquiry (He Ara Oranga) held 2018; $1.9b committed 2019-2023; Mental Health Commission re-established. Primary-care services (Access and Choice) expanded, but a 2021 government mid-term review found weak accountability and the Ministry of Health did not see itself as leading the programme; in 2022 advocates said little had changed for many people and specialist services were unchanged in five years.

labour.promise: No new taxes before the 2020 election (Tax Working Group changes only from 2021) other than those specified
labour.detail: After National's 'tax' attacks Ardern announced a week before the election that any Tax Working Group changes would not take effect until after 2020. No new broad taxes were introduced 2017-20; specified measures (regional fuel tax, fuel excise rises, bright-line extension to 5 years) went ahead.

labour.promise: Use the Tax Working Group to make the system 'fairer', including a possible capital gains tax
labour.detail: The TWG (chaired by Sir Michael Cullen) recommended a broad CGT in February 2019. On 17 April 2019 Ardern ruled it out, citing no consensus in the coalition (NZ First opposed) and no mandate, and said she would not revisit it as leader - while saying she still believed in it.

labour.promise: Charge commercial users (including irrigators) a royalty for water
labour.detail: Dropped in coalition talks with NZ First in October 2017 - Ardern said it was the one concession Labour made. A narrower bottled-water export royalty was put in the agreement.

labour.promise: Raise the minimum wage to $20 an hour by 2021
Abolish 90-day trial periods
labour.detail: Compromise with NZ First: trials kept for firms with fewer than 20 employees and removed for larger firms.

labour.promise: Re-enter the Pike River mine drift and recover remains/evidence where practicable
labour.detail: Pike River Recovery Agency re-entered and explored the 2.2-2.4km drift; work was completed and the drift sealed in December 2021, with the agency disestablished July 2022. No remains were recovered and the mine workings were not entered; costs roughly doubled to over $50m. Winston Peters later alleged the government broke its word; Little said it delivered what was promised.

labour.promise: Add 1,800 new police officers over three years (NZ First coalition agreement)
labour.detail: Government declared the target met in November 2019 (1,825 graduates deployed since October 2017) after redefining it as 1,800 graduates rather than 1,800 over attrition; the net increase in police staff was about 1,000.

labour.promise: Plant one billion trees over ten years (NZ First coalition agreement)
labour.detail: The count includes commercial replanting; an MPI Cabinet paper estimated the programme itself would contribute less than a third. The dedicated One Billion Trees Fund closed in June 2021 having directly funded ~48 million trees. The NZ Conservation Authority warned in 2020 natives were ~12% of plantings against a two-thirds Cabinet target. No independent, audited tally of progress toward the billion was found.

labour.promise: $1 billion a year Provincial Growth Fund (NZ First coalition agreement)
labour.detail: Around $3b allocated over the term. Job-creation claims were contested (1News 2019 analysis; the Auditor-General questioned job calculations in 2020); a later review credited ~8,400 jobs.

labour.promise: Pass a Zero Carbon Act with an independent Climate Change Commission (Green C&S agreement)
labour.detail: Passed 7 November 2019 with National's support at third reading; Climate Change Commission established.

labour.promise: No new offshore oil and gas exploration permits
labour.detail: Not a 2017 manifesto line; announced in April 2018 and legislated (Crown Minerals (Petroleum) Amendment Act 2018). Existing permits unaffected. Reversed by the National-led government's Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025 (in force August 2025).

labour.promise: Make rivers and lakes swimmable within a generation
labour.detail: Essential Freshwater package (2020) set new national standards, but the swimmability goal had no statutory deadline and a 2020 Herald assessment graded it D for ambition. Parts were later wound back by the 2023-26 government.

labour.promise: Cheaper doctors' visits; free GP visits for under-14s
labour.detail: Free under-14 visits and lower fees for Community Services Card holders from December 2018.

labour.promise: Scrap National Standards and charter schools
labour.detail: National Standards scrapped December 2017; charter school law repealed 2018 with existing schools converted to state 'special character' schools.

labour.promise: Resume contributions to the NZ Super Fund and keep the pension age at 65
labour.detail: Contributions resumed; age kept at 65.

labour.promise: Raise the refugee quota to 1,500
labour.detail: Quota raised (to 1,500 from July 2020; resettlement disrupted by COVID).

labour.promise: Royal Commission into abuse in state care
labour.detail: Established 2018; final report delivered 2024.

labour.promise: Take abortion out of the Crimes Act
labour.detail: Abortion Legislation Act 2020 passed (conscience vote) in March 2020.

labour.promise: Hold a binding referendum on recreational cannabis by 2020 (Green C&S agreement)
labour.detail: Held with the 2020 election; 'No' won 50.7% to 48.4%. Labour took no party position; Ardern revealed only after the vote that she had voted yes - some experts said her silence may have been decisive.

labour.promise: Repeal the 'three strikes' sentencing law
labour.detail: Abandoned in June 2018 when NZ First refused support; repealed in 2022 once Labour governed alone (Three Strikes Legislation Repeal Act 2022). Reinstated by the National-led government in 2024.

labour.promise: Ihumātao: no building on the land while talks continue, and a negotiated solution (Ardern, July 2019)
labour.detail: Development halted in 2019; in December 2020 the Crown agreed to buy the land from Fletcher Building for $29.9m (outside the Treaty settlement process) under the Land for Housing Programme, with a Kīngitanga/Crown/Auckland Council MoU. Critics raised precedent concerns for full and final settlements.

labour.promise: Merge the 16 polytechnics and industry training organisations into one national institute (Te Pūkenga) to make vocational education financially sustainable
labour.detail: Not a 2017 manifesto commitment; went further than the options consulted on. Merger took effect 2020-2023, but Te Pūkenga ran large deficits (forecast up to $110m in 2022), suffered leadership turnover and missed transition milestones. The coalition government is breaking it up; standalone polytechnics resumed from 2026 with Te Pūkenga disestablished at the end of 2026.

labour.promise: COVID-19 elimination strategy ('go hard and go early')
labour.detail: Elimination achieved in 2020 and most of 2021, with among the lowest death rates in the OECD and negative excess mortality to early 2023 (Royal Commission phase 1, Nov 2024). The strategy was abandoned in October 2021 after Delta; the Commission's phase 2 (March 2026) found the response 'broadly effective but flawed', criticising lockdown length, mandates' social-cohesion costs and the slow exit.

labour.promise: COVID wage subsidy to keep workers attached to employers
labour.detail: More than $13b paid March-December 2020 (about $19b by end of 2021). The Auditor-General found 'much to commend' but weak post-payment verification and urged recovery/prosecution of misuse.

labour.promise: New 39% top tax rate on income over $180,000 (affecting ~2% of earners)
labour.detail: Legislated December 2020, in force 1 April 2021.

labour.promise: No other tax changes beyond the 39% rate - specifically no extension of the bright-line test (Grant Robertson)
labour.detail: In March 2021 the government extended the bright-line test from 5 to 10 years for existing homes and began phasing out interest deductibility for residential landlords. Robertson admitted he had been 'too definitive' in ruling out a bright-line extension during the campaign; he argued the bright-line test is not a new tax. (The coalition restored interest deductibility from 2025; Labour said in Sept 2026 it would not change it again.)

labour.promise: No wealth tax ('I won't allow it to happen as Prime Minister' - Ardern)
labour.detail: No wealth tax introduced 2020-23 despite Green pressure; David Parker's later work on one was shut down by Hipkins in 2023.

labour.promise: Double minimum sick leave from 5 to 10 days
labour.detail: Legislation introduced December 2020; 10 days in force from July 2021.

labour.promise: New Matariki public holiday from 2022
labour.detail: First observed 24 June 2022 (Te Kāhui o Matariki Public Holiday Act 2022).

labour.promise: Ban conversion therapy
labour.detail: Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Act passed February 2022 (strong cross-party support).

labour.promise: Introduce Fair Pay Agreements (sector-wide bargaining)
labour.detail: Delayed in the first term (NZ First opposed); Fair Pay Agreements Act passed October 2022. No FPA was concluded before the coalition repealed the Act under urgency in December 2023.

labour.promise: Free trades training and apprenticeships (TTAF) and Apprenticeship Boost
labour.detail: Apprenticeship fees removed from 1 July 2020 (TTAF ran to end of 2022); Apprenticeship Boost subsidy for employers.

labour.promise: 8,000 more public and transitional homes (Budget 2020, campaigned on in 2020)
labour.detail: Public housing additions continued at the highest rate in decades (Labour: 13,000+ public homes and 4,000+ transitional places 2017-23). No independent final audit of the specific 8,000 package was found, and new-build share is disputed.

labour.promise: Progress Auckland light rail now NZ First is gone
labour.detail: A $14.6b tunnelled scheme was endorsed in 2022 and a delivery company set up, but no construction began before the 2023 election; the project was cancelled in January 2024.

labour.promise: Three Waters reform would be voluntary (councils could opt out)
labour.detail: The government initially said participation was optional, then in mid/late 2021 made the transfer of water assets to new entities mandatory. Ardern denied misleading councils.

labour.promise: Reform drinking, waste and storm water into large publicly owned entities (Three Waters)
labour.detail: Water Services Entities Act 2022 passed in December 2022 with Labour votes only (including a controversial, later-removed entrenchment clause). Hipkins' April 2023 reset replaced 4 entities with 10 and delayed the start to 2026. Whether there was an electoral mandate was contested. Fully repealed by the coalition in February 2024 ('Local Water Done Well').

labour.promise: Replace the 20 district health boards with Health NZ (Te Whatu Ora) and a Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora)
labour.detail: Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022; new entities from 1 July 2022. Outcomes contested: Health NZ overspent (a $722m deficit for 2023/24), and in July 2024 the coalition replaced its board with a commissioner, blaming an over-centralised model; Labour called this 'political spin' and pointed to inflation and pay settlements. Te Aka Whai Ora was abolished in June 2024.

labour.promise: Smokefree generation: ban tobacco sales to anyone born after 1 Jan 2009, cut retailers and nicotine
labour.detail: Law passed December 2022; the three main measures were repealed by the coalition in early 2024 before taking effect.

labour.promise: Clean Car Discount (feebate) and clean car import standard
labour.detail: Discount operated 2021-2023 and the import standard was legislated; the discount was ended by the incoming government at the end of 2023. Hipkins had already dropped the related Clean Car Upgrade scheme.

labour.promise: Merge RNZ and TVNZ into a new public media entity
labour.detail: Scrapped in Hipkins' February 2023 'policy bonfire' after about $23m had been spent.

labour.promise: Social unemployment insurance scheme (with business and unions)
labour.detail: Shelved in February 2023 'until the economy improves'; not revived.

labour.promise: Biofuels mandate for transport fuel
labour.detail: Dropped February 2023 because it would raise fuel prices.

labour.promise: Hate speech law reform (post-Christchurch Royal Commission)
labour.detail: Withdrawn and referred to the Law Commission in February 2023.

labour.promise: Lower the voting age to 16 for local elections
labour.detail: Dropped in Hipkins' 2023 reprioritisation. Labour's 2026 platform again supports 16- and 17-year-olds voting in local elections.

labour.promise: Remove the $5 prescription co-payment
labour.detail: Took effect 1 July 2023; reinstated by the coalition from July 2024 for most adults. Labour promises to remove it again in 2026.

labour.promise: Free public transport for 5-12 year-olds and half-price fares for under-25s
labour.detail: In place from July 2023; central funding withdrawn by the coalition and the concessions ended 30 April 2024.

labour.promise: 'Under a government I lead there will be no wealth or capital gains tax' (Hipkins, July 2023)
labour.detail: After the defeat Hipkins said tax was 'back on the table' (Nov 2023). In October 2025 Labour adopted a 28% capital gains tax on residential and commercial property (excluding the family home and farms) from July 2027, to fund free GP visits - with Hipkins still leader.

labour.promise: Remove GST from fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables from 1 April 2024
labour.detail: Not implemented (Labour lost). It does not appear among Labour's 2026 policies as listed by policy.nz (October 2026); we did not find a formal statement dropping it, so treat 'abandoned' as 'not carried forward'. Robertson reportedly opposed it in 2023.

labour.promise: Free basic dental care for under-30s (18-23 from July 2025; 18-29 from July 2026)
labour.detail: Not implemented (Labour lost). Not among Labour's 2026 policies as listed by policy.nz; 2026 health offer instead centres on free GP visits ('Medicard') and free prescriptions.

labour.promise: 6,000 more public homes by 2027
labour.detail: Not implemented (Labour lost). Carried forward in 2026 as 'at least 6,000 more social housing places over the next 4 years'.

labour.promise: Rest of the 2023 nine-point pledge card (20 hours free ECE for 2-year-olds, Working for Families boost, 300 more police, partner paid leave, financial literacy, India trade mission, permanent Apprenticeship Boost)
labour.detail: Untested because Labour lost. Some items reappear in 2026 (Apprenticeship Boost restored and expanded); others are not in the 2026 platform.

labour.promise: 28% capital gains tax on residential and commercial property (excluding the family home and farms) from July 2027, not retrospective
labour.detail: Labour's revenue base for its health offer; a reversal of Hipkins' 2023 pledge.

labour.promise: Up to three free GP visits a year for everyone (Medicard), free maternity scans, free cervical screening 25-69
Remove the $5 prescription charge (again)
NZ Future Fund to invest in infrastructure and NZ businesses (Temasek-style)
labour.detail: Labour said in May 2026 it would not release the fund's costing or which state assets would be included until after the election.

labour.promise: $20 weekly public transport fare cap in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch ($10 elsewhere) from July 2027
labour.detail: Labour costed it at $65m a year; economists Sam Warburton and Brad Olsen estimated $91-112m.

labour.promise: Return to surplus by 2029/30 and cut net debt to around 20% of GDP; independent Parliamentary Budget Office; restore wellbeing reporting and the Reserve Bank's dual mandate
Rule out raising GST in 2027; oppose fuel excise increases; no change to landlord interest deductibility
$4b over four years for at least 6,000 more social housing places, school and hospital repairs
Write off 10% of eligible graduates' student loans ($583.4m over four years)
Restore the pay equity regime and give 65,000 care and support workers a pay rise ($2.5b over four years)
Make employer KiwiSaver contributions compulsory and raise the minimum contribution to 6%
Force Foodstuffs and Woolworths to separate wholesale from retail; ban excessive pricing ('price gouging')
Repeal the Regulatory Standards Act within the first 100 days
Send an under-16 social media ban bill to select committee within 100 days
Pause the coalition's NCEA replacement and curriculum overhaul; restore school boards' Treaty obligations; 1,000 more teacher aides; locally made school lunches
Scrap youth offender boot camps; create a corporate homicide offence
Recognise Palestine, sanction Israel, stay out of AUKUS, lift aid towards 0.7% of GDP
Guarantee a job for every NZ-trained graduate nurse
Increase the minimum wage every year

act.promise: Introduce charter (partnership) schools
act.detail: Secured in ACT's 2011 support agreement with National. The enabling Education Amendment Bill was introduced in October 2012 and became law. The first five partnership schools (kura hourua) opened in Auckland and Northland in February 2014. Between 2014 and 2017 the authorisation board approved 17 of 111 applications. The Labour-led government abolished the model in 2018, and all 12 remaining schools became state-integrated or special-character schools by September 2018.

act.promise: A low, near-flat income tax (about 15%, with the first $25,000 tax-free for people who opt out of state cover)
act.detail: Never enacted. By 2021 ACT no longer advocated a flat tax, and it campaigned in 2020 and 2023 for lower graduated rates instead (see the 2020 and 2023 tax entries).

act.promise: Regulatory responsibility / regulatory standards law setting principles for good law-making
act.made: Long-standing: 2006 member's bill (Hide), 2011 support agreement, 2023 coalition agreement
act.detail: ACT proposed this for almost two decades. Rodney Hide's 2006 member's bill and the 2011 Regulatory Standards Bill (from the Regulatory Responsibility Taskforce) both failed. It was finally delivered under the 2023 coalition agreement: the Regulatory Standards Bill was introduced on 19 May 2025 and passed its third reading on 13 November 2025, 68–55, with only National, ACT and NZ First in favour. It took effect on 1 January 2026, and the first Regulatory Standards Board members were appointed in April 2026. Public opposition was very strong: the Ministry estimated that 88% of almost 23,000 submissions on the discussion document opposed it, and about 99% of submissions to the select committee were against it. NZ First, which voted for the bill, has since pledged to repeal it.

act.promise: Three-strikes sentencing for burglary
act.made: 2014 election (announced by leader Jamie Whyte, March 2014); repeated 2026
act.detail: Never enacted. The three-strikes regime reinstated in 2024 covers serious violent and sexual offences, not burglary. In July 2026 deputy leader Nicole McKee announced that ACT would again campaign on adding burglary to it.

act.promise: Review and replace the Resource Management Act
act.detail: The National-led coalition repealed Labour's replacement laws (the Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act) in December 2023. In September 2026 Parliament passed two replacement laws, the Planning Act 2026 and the Natural Environment Act 2026, sponsored by National's Chris Bishop. ACT's Simon Court served as Parliamentary Under-Secretary for RMA reform. The RMA, as amended, remains the main law during a four-year transition, so the change is legislated but not yet in full effect.

act.promise: Expand partnership (charter) schools
act.detail: David Seymour became Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Education Minister with responsibility for charter schools. More schools were approved and opened between 2014 and 2017, and a support entity, E Tipu E Rea, was funded in 2016. All of this was reversed by the incoming Labour-led government in 2017–18.

act.promise: Legalise assisted dying (End of Life Choice Bill)
act.detail: Seymour's member's bill passed its third reading in November 2019. To win NZ First's votes, an amendment made the law subject to a binding referendum, which passed 63–57. Voters approved it at the 2020 referendum, and the End of Life Choice Act came into force on 7 November 2021. This was ACT's biggest policy win during its one-MP years (2011–2020).

act.promise: Permanent income tax cuts, including cutting the 30% middle-income rate to 17.5%
act.detail: Not delivered during 2020–23, when ACT was in opposition. In 2023 the coalition adopted National's smaller tax-threshold package rather than ACT's rate structure (see the 2023 tax entry).

act.promise: Abolish 'demographic' ministries: the Ministry for Women, Ministry for Pacific Peoples and Ministry for Ethnic Communities, plus the Human Rights Commission
act.detail: Not included in the 2023 coalition agreement, and all three ministries still exist with ministers in the National-led government. ACT's 2026 fiscal plan again proposes abolishing 'demographic' ministries.

act.promise: Abolish the Māori electorates and reduce Parliament from 120 to 100 MPs
act.detail: Not in the 2023 coalition agreement and not progressed in government.

act.promise: Referendum on the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, made a condition of coalition with National
act.detail: In 2022 ACT said the referendum would be a condition of forming a government with National. It dropped that condition in the 2023 coalition negotiations. Instead, the agreement only committed National to support a Treaty Principles Bill up to and through select committee.

act.promise: Pass a Treaty Principles Act defining the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi
act.detail: The narrow coalition commitment was honoured. The bill was introduced in November 2024 and passed its first reading on 14 November 2024, 68–54, with National and NZ First support. That vote prompted the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti. The select committee received about 300,000 written submissions, a record, and around 90% opposed the bill. On 10 April 2025 it was voted down at second reading, 112–11, with only ACT in favour. National and NZ First had said beforehand they would vote against it at that stage. ACT's actual goal, a Treaty Principles law, was therefore not achieved.

act.promise: A Ministry for Regulation and a Minister for Regulation to cut red tape
act.detail: The Ministry for Regulation was established on 1 March 2024, funded partly by disestablishing the Productivity Commission, with Seymour as the first Minister for Regulation. It has carried out sector reviews, starting with early childhood education in 2024. It also drew criticism over staff salaries (70 permanent staff averaging about $150,000 in April 2025).

act.promise: Bring back charter schools and let state schools convert to charter schools
act.detail: Legislation passed on 25 September 2024. Budget 2024 allocated $153m to convert 35 state schools and open 15 new charter schools in 2025–26 (50 in total). The first seven schools opened in February 2025 and 18 were operating by July 2026, with 1,732 students on 1 July 2026. The first state-school conversion happened only on 12 October 2026. The law is in place, but the scale is well short of the 50-school plan.

act.promise: Restore interest deductibility for residential landlords, faster than National proposed
act.detail: Legislated in March 2024: 80% deductibility from 1 April 2024 and 100% from 1 April 2025.

act.promise: Tenancy law changes including pet bonds
act.detail: The Residential Tenancies Amendment legislation passed in December 2024. It introduced pet bonds, restored 90-day no-cause terminations and shortened some notice periods. Renters' United criticised the changes.

act.promise: Reinstate the three-strikes law
act.detail: The Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act passed on 13 December 2024, introduced by ACT's Nicole McKee, and has applied since 17 June 2025. It covers the same serious violent and sexual offences as the 2010 law plus a new strangulation offence, with changes intended to make it more workable.

act.promise: Tougher action on gangs (gang patch ban, gang membership as an aggravating factor)
act.detail: The gang patch ban and the aggravating-factor laws passed on 19 September 2024 with National, ACT and NZ First support. These were National's flagship policies, which ACT backed. Some critics noted a tension with ACT's free-expression principles.

act.promise: Rewrite the Arms Act 1983 and move the firearms regulator out of Police
act.detail: Nicole McKee's Arms Bill was introduced in December 2025 and passed its first reading with broad support. It passed its third reading on 29 July 2026 and received Royal assent on 4 August 2026 as the Arms Act 2026, replacing the 1983 Act. The new law sets up a firearms regulator separate from the Police Commissioner, bars gang members from holding licences and gives the regulator infringement powers. Commentators noted the final vote was much less unanimous than the 2019 reforms. Implementation is phased.

act.promise: Review the firearms registry
act.detail: The review was in the coalition agreement. In May 2025 ACT invoked the 'agree to disagree' clause after National declined McKee's call for a more 'thorough and independent' review of the registry.

act.promise: Shrink the public service back to its 2017 size by cutting back-office functions
act.detail: Thousands of public-sector roles were cut. Reported totals ranged from about 3,745 by May 2024 to over 9,000 by 2025, depending on the source and what was counted. Even so, Public Service Commission data show 63,912 full-time-equivalent staff at 30 June 2026, against 63,117 in June 2023 and a peak of 65,699 in December 2023. The 2017 public service was about 13,000 FTE smaller than in 2022, roughly 47,000. Headcount has not returned to anything near 2017 levels.

act.promise: Larger, flatter income tax cuts (ACT's tax plan)
act.detail: The coalition agreement said ACT's flat-tax principles would be 'considered'. What was enacted was National's package: about $14 billion of income tax relief in Budget 2024, worth $4–$40 a fortnight to workers earning over $14,000. ACT's rate structure was not adopted.

act.promise: 90-day trial periods for all employers
act.detail: Passed on 21 December 2023 as part of the 100-day plan.

act.promise: Repeal Fair Pay Agreements
act.detail: Repealed on 14 December 2023 (a shared National and ACT policy).

act.promise: Narrow the Reserve Bank's mandate to price stability
act.detail: The Reserve Bank's dual mandate was removed in December 2023.

act.promise: Reverse the ban on live animal exports by sea
act.detail: On 10 March 2026 ACT's Associate Agriculture Minister Andrew Hoggard said he could not get Cabinet agreement and the ban would not be overturned this term. He admitted he had earlier promised legislation by then.

act.promise: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and abolish the Climate Change Commission
act.detail: Not included in the 2023 coalition agreement, and the Act and Commission remain. In August and September 2026 ACT revived both pledges, including scrapping the net-zero target.

act.promise: Deliver public services based on need, not race
act.detail: On 13 September 2024 the Cabinet Office directed that public services be delivered on the basis of 'need' rather than 'race', and the target for Māori business procurement was dropped. Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority) was disestablished in 2024. After ACT pressure, ACC's Māori and Pasifika health targets were scrapped in May 2025. Some ethnicity-based programmes remain, and ACT is campaigning in 2026 for further law changes.

act.promise: Repeal section 7AA (Treaty obligations) of the Oranga Tamariki Act
act.made: 2023 coalition agreement (ACT's Karen Chhour, Minister for Children)
act.detail: The repeal passed on 3 April 2025. This was despite a May 2024 Waitangi Tribunal finding that it breached Treaty guarantees and related Court of Appeal litigation.

act.promise: Make the free school lunch programme cheaper
act.detail: Associate Education Minister Seymour redesigned the scheme in 2024: bulk-purchased meals for intermediate and secondary students, with a stated saving of about $130m a year. The new supplier model drew widespread complaints about meal quality. Funding was extended for 2027 ($212m), with changes flagged for 2028. Cabinet also dropped the programme's Māori name.

act.promise: Reform Pharmac to fund more medicines faster and give patients a greater voice
act.detail: Seymour took ministerial responsibility for Pharmac as Associate Health Minister. His July 2024 letter of expectations told Pharmac to stop considering the Treaty and to involve patient groups more, and one director resigned over it. Budget 2024 added $604m over four years for 54 medicines, including 26 cancer treatments (National's cancer-drug pledge). No structural change to Pharmac's funding model was legislated. ACT's 2026 platform again promises to raise Pharmac's share of the health budget; sources differ on the target (10%, 12% or 13% by 2033).

act.promise: A four-year parliamentary term, subject to a referendum
act.detail: The narrow commitment was met: the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) bill passed its first reading on 5 March 2025. In February 2026, however, the government decided not to progress it this term, and the planned 2026 referendum was dropped.

act.promise: Shared deputy prime ministership (Seymour from 31 May 2025)
act.detail: Seymour took over as Deputy Prime Minister from Winston Peters on 31 May 2025, the first ACT MP to hold the role.

act.promise: Raise the NZ Super eligibility age by three months a year (with compassionate access for people in physically demanding jobs) and pause Super Fund contributions
act.detail: Part of ACT's 2026 fiscal plan, alongside returning non-welfare spending to 2017 per-capita levels, $653m of disability-benefit savings and abolishing demographic ministries. National kept the age at 65 under its 2023 deal with NZ First.

act.promise: Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years and introduce a training wage for under-20s
act.detail: Announced on 15 September 2026 as part of ACT's small business policy.

act.promise: Disestablish the Waitangi Tribunal once outstanding historical claims are resolved
act.detail: Announced on 10 September 2026. It would apply once all claims lodged by 1 September 2008 are resolved.

act.promise: Tighter immigration rules: deport serious non-citizen offenders, a five-year benefit stand-down for new residents, a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, and an end to the permanent resident visa category
